title: Hammira's Guest at Ranthambhore
subtitle: The Siege of Oaths at Ranthambhore
moral: An oath may outlive the ruler who keeps it.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khaza'in-ul-Futuh, c. 1311 CE; Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, c. 1357 CE
sources.note: Sultanate-side accounts of Alauddin Khalji's siege.

sources.citation: Nayachandra Suri, Hammira Mahakavya, c. 1400-1420 CE
sources.note: Later Jain/Sanskrit heroic poem preserving Rajput memory, not an eyewitness chronicle.

sources.citation: Dasharatha Sharma, Early Chahamana Dynasties (1959); Aditya Malik on Hammira memory

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of Ranthambhore fort rising from sheer cliffs under a stormy sky

dialogue.text: At Ranthambhore, a Rajput king chose to shelter the Sultan’s own rebel Mongols—and kept his oath until the fort, his line, and his life were all ground under the siege.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot from a bird’s-eye view

dialogue.text: At the turn of the fourteenth century, Ranthambhore stood like a stone ship on a sea of ravines—one of north India’s strongest forts and the heart of the Chahamana kingdom.

panels.shot: medium shot in a dim audience hall

dialogue.text: Hammira, the Chahamana ruler, had grown up in the shadow of the Delhi Sultanate’s rise, watching his forefathers lose Ajmer and Delhi yet cling to these hills.

panels.shot: tight medium of Hammira with a messenger

dialogue.text: To the north, Alauddin Khalji—fresh from Devagiri and Gujarat—was turning Delhi into a center of wealth and iron law, wary above all of the Mongol horsemen who kept testing his frontiers.

panels.shot: wide shot of a winter plain near Delhi

dialogue.text: Some Mongols had entered the Sultan’s service, guarding his frontiers. But in 1299, a faction rebelled near Delhi, their rising crushed, their leaders hunted.
Some of these fugitive Mongols rode south and east, seeking asylum. The chronicles record that a band reached Ranthambhore and asked Hammira for shelter.
Here the traditions agree: Hammira accepted them. A Hindu Rajput king opened his great fort to Muslim Mongols who had defied the Muslim Sultan of Delhi.

panels.shot: wide overhead shot of Delhi court

dialogue.text: When news reached Alauddin that his Mongol rebels had found refuge with Hammira, he demanded their surrender. It was a test of submission as much as of loyalty.
Hammira refused to deliver them. The court kavyas later frame it as a matter of honor and asylum; the Sultanate chroniclers record simply that he did not obey.
Alauddin chose war. In 1299 he sent his general Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan towards Ranthambhore, beginning a campaign that would stretch on and harden into siege.
Hammira’s forces met them in the field more than once. The details differ across texts, but the core remains: skirmishes, sorties, and the long drawing of a noose.
In the fighting around Ranthambhore, Nusrat Khan was killed. Even Alauddin’s court poet Amir Khusrau notes this loss—a blow that turned the Sultan’s attention wholly to this siege.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of Alauddin outside Ranthambhore

dialogue.text: Alauddin came in person. By 1301, the Sultan had ringed Ranthambhore with his own presence, determined that the fort and its defiant ruler must fall.
The siege tightened. Siege towers crept forward, trenches were dug, and the hill-fort’s defenders watched their world slowly encircled by canvas, wood, and steel.
Inside, food and hope thinned. Khusrau and Barani both speak of famine within the fort—grain dwindling, animals slaughtered, men and women facing hunger as keen as any spear.
The garrison was not only warriors. The siege pressed on merchants, artisans, priests, and families, all trapped atop the hill, each day a little more desperate than the last.

panels.shot: medium in a dim royal chamber

dialogue.text: Our details are thinnest for the nights of decision. The Jain mahakavya imagines long speeches on dharma; the Sultanate chronicles are curt. All agree: surrender was not chosen.
Later accounts speak of jauhar at Ranthambhore—women choosing death by fire as the walls neared breach. The numbers and scenes are literary, but the tradition of such an ending is old and persistent.
Hammira is said to have ridden out in a last sortie, choosing to die in battle. The chronicles agree that he fell in defeat, his kingdom ending in a single furious rush.
Ranthambhore fell. Alauddin’s banners rose over its walls, and the Chahamana stronghold passed into Sultanate control after months of hunger, siegecraft, and unbroken pressure.

panels.shot: symbolic close-up on an empty throne and sword

dialogue.text: The Hammira Mahakavya would, a century later, sing him as a martyr to his vow; Khusrau listed him among Alauddin’s conquered. Between them lies a simple fact: an oath outlived the man who kept it.
